label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $K$ be a number field and $d\geq 2$. There are only finitely many monic centred
 PCF  polynomials of degree $d$ with coefficients
in $K^{\mathrm{cyc}}$.
head: environment

label: thm:laurent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{thm:laurent}
If $T\subseteq G$ is an infinite set of torsion points, then there is a positive-dimensional torsion coset $\eta H \subseteq G$ such that $\eta H\cap T$ is Zariski dense in $\eta H$.
head: environment

label: prop:house
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:archak
title: Proof
body_md:
Part~\eqref{it:one} is contained in \cite{Ingram}, but not quite explicitly. Let $\sigma_j = \sigma_j(c_1, \dots, c_{d-1})$ denote the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree $j$, and set
\[g(z)=\frac{1}{d}z^d-\frac{\sigma_1}{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots +(-1)^{d-1}\sigma_{d-1}z\]
so that
\[g'(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{d-1}(z-c_i).\]
If $g$ is PCF, then \cite[Lemma~2.5]{Ingram}  shows that
 $|c_i|\leq \Delta_v$, for some $M_\mathbb{Q}$-constant $\Delta$ (which is $e^{\delta}$ in the notation of that paper), and for every extension of $|\cdot|_v$ to $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (applying the lemma to a Galois conjugate of $g$ if necessary). Increasing $\Delta$, we may assume that $\Delta_v\geq 1$ for all $v$. Now, let $\psi(z)=\alpha z + \beta$ with $\alpha^{d-1}=d$ and $\beta=(c_1+\cdots +c_{d-1})/(d-1)$, so that \[f(z)=g^{\psi}(z)=\psi^{-1}\circ g\circ \psi(z)=z^d+a_{d-2}z^{d-2}+\cdots +a_0\] is monic and centred. 
Expanding, the coefficients are given by
\[
a_k = \frac{\alpha^{k-1}}{k}
   \sum_{j=0}^{d-k} (-1)^{j} \binom{d-1-j}{k-1} \sigma_j \beta^{d-k-j}
\]
for $1\leq k\leq d-2$, and
\[
a_0 = \frac{g(\beta) - \beta}{\alpha}
=\frac{1}{\alpha} \left( \sum_{m=1}^{d} \frac{(-1)^{d-m}}{m} \sigma_{d-m} \beta^{m} - \beta \right).
\]
So for $1\leq k\leq d-2$ we have for archimedean places
\begin{align}
|a_k|_v&\leq \left|\frac{d^{(k-1)/(d-1)}}{k}\right|_v\sum_{j=0}^{d-k}  \binom{d-1-j}{k-1}\left| \sigma_j\, \beta^{\,d-k-j}\right|_v \nonumber\\
&\leq \left|\frac{d^{(k-1)/(d-1)}}{k}\right|_v\sum_{j=0}^{d-k}  \binom{d-1-j}{k-1}\binom{d-1}{j}\Delta_\infty^{d-k},\label{eq:archak}
\end{align}
and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:archa0}|a_0|_v \leq d^{-1/(d-1)} \sum_{m=1}^{d}\binom{d-1}{m-1} \frac{1}{m} \Delta_\infty^{d} + \Delta_\infty.
\end{equation}
Choosing $N_v$ to be the maximum of the upper bounds in~\eqref{eq:archak} and~\eqref{eq:archa0} for $1\leq k \leq d-2$, we have $|a_k|_v\leq N_v$ for all $k$ with $N_v$ depending just on $d$.

For $v$ non-archimedean, we have $|\sigma_j|_v\leq \Delta_v^j$ and $|\beta|_v\leq |d-1|_v^{-1}\Delta_v$, and so
\begin{align}
|a_k|_v&\leq \left|\frac{d^{(k-1)/(d-1)}}{k}\right|_v\max_{j=0}^{d-k} \left| \sigma_j\, \beta^{d-k-j}\right|_v\nonumber \\
&\leq \left|\frac{d^{(k-1)/(d-1)}}{k(d-1)^{d-k}}\right|_v\Delta_v^{d-k}\label{eq:naak}
\end{align}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:naa0}|a_0|_v \leq |d|_v^{-1/(d-1)}|d-1|_v^{-d}\Delta_v^{d}\max_{1\leq m\leq d}|m|_v^{-1},\end{equation}
and so we may again choose $N_v$ to satisfy $|a_k|_v\leq N_v$ for all $k$, noting that the upper bounds in~\eqref{eq:naak} and~\eqref{eq:naa0} are 1 for those $v$ with $\Delta_v=1$ and $|k|_v=1$ for all $1\leq k\leq d$, which is all but finitely many.


So $|a_i|_v\leq N_v$ for some $M_\mathbb{Q}$-constant $N$ depending only on $d$ and $\Delta$, and we may take $N_v\geq 1$. But every monic centred polynomial is the image of some $g$ under this map, and so we have our first claim. Indeed, if $f$ is monic and centred, let $p$ be a fixed point of $f$, and let $g=\psi\circ f\circ \psi^{-1}$ with $\psi(z)=\alpha(z-p)$. Then $g(0)=0$ and $g$ has leading coefficient $1/d$, so $g$ has the form above, and since the critical points of $f$ sum to zero, the critical points $c_i$ of $g$ have mean $-\alpha p$, so that $\psi(z)=\alpha z+\beta$ as above. Since being PCF is invariant under conjugation, the bound on the $c_i$ applies.

For~\eqref{it:two} we recall the standard escape argument. If $v$ is non-archimedean and $|a_k|_v\leq N_v$ for all $k$, then $|z|_v>N_v\geq 1$ gives
\[|f(z)|_v=|z|^d_v\cdot |1+a_{d-2}z^{-2}+\cdots +a_0z^{-d}|_v=|z|_v^d>|z|_v,\]
and so by induction $z$ is not preperiodic for $f$. It follows for $f$ PCF that $|f^k(c)|\leq N_v$ for all $k\geq 0$ and all critical points $c$ of $f$.

In the case where $v$ is archimedean, with $|a_k|_v\leq N_v$, we see that $|z|_v> 2(d-1)N_v$ gives 
\[|1+a_{d-2}z^{-2}+\cdots +a_0z^{-d}|_v\geq \frac{1}{2}\]
and hence
\[|f(z)|_v\geq \frac{1}{2} |z|_v^d> |z|_v.\]
Again, such a point cannot be preperiodic, so we must have $|f^k(c)|_v\leq 2(d-1)N_v$ for all $f'(c)=0$ and all $k\geq 0$. So we set $M_v=4(d-1)N_v$ for archimedean places, and $M_v=N_v$ for non-archimedean. By the triangle and ultrametric inequalities, we have both $|f^n(c)|\leq M_v$ and $|f^n(c)-f^m(c)|\leq M_v$ for all $n, m$, and $v$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Dvornicich--Zannier~\cite[Theorem~L]{DZ} prove that for every $B'>0$ there are a finite set $E=\{c_1, ..., c_s\}\subseteq K$ and an integer $N\geq 1$ such that every algebraic integer in $K^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ all of whose conjugates have absolute value at most $B'$ can be written as $\sum_{
u=1}^{b}c_{j_
u}\xi_
u$ with $b\leq N$, each $c_{j_
u}\in E$, and each $\xi_
u$ a root of unity. In general, choose an integer $D\geq 1$ such that $|D|_v\leq M_v^{-1}$ for all finite places $v$, and let $M'=\max_{v\in M_K^\infty} DM_v$. Then our hypothesis implies that $D\alpha$ is an algebraic integer all of whose conjugates have absolute value at most $M'$, so we may write $D\alpha = \sum_{
u=1}^b c_{j_
u} \xi_
u$ with $b\leq N$. Now let $L$ be the linear form in the $sN$ variables $x_{j, k}$, $1\leq j\leq s$ and $1\leq k\leq N$, given by
\[L(x)=\sum_{j=1}^s\sum_{k=1}^N  rac{c_j}{D}x_{j, k}.\]
Placing each term $c_{j_
u}\xi_
u$ in an unused variable $x_{j_
u, k}$, and setting the remaining variables to zero, we obtain $\alpha=L(\zeta)$ with each $\zeta_{j, k}$ either zero or a root of unity.

label: lem:hajos
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hajos}
Let $x\in\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^m (\mathbb{C})$, and let $F$ be a non-zero Laurent polynomial in $m$ variables expressible as a linear combination of at most $T$ monomials.
Then
\[\operatorname{ord}_x\left(F\right)\leq T-1.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We start with the case $m=1$, which is well-known but we prove for completeness by induction on $T$. Of course, for $T=1$ we have that $F$ is a (non-zero) monomial, and so does not vanish on $\mathbb{C}^\times$. Now, if the claim is known for $T=k$, consider
$F=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \beta_i u^{r_i}$. If any $\beta_i$ vanishes or if the exponents are not distinct, we can re-write this expression with fewer terms and apply the induction hypothesis directly, so without loss of generality suppose that $r_1>r_2\cdots >r_{k+1}$ with $\beta_i\neq 0$ for all $i$. If $F(x)\neq 0$ there is nothing to prove, so suppose $F(x)=0$. For $x\neq 0$ any polynomial $P$ vanishing at $x$ we have $\operatorname{ord}_x(P)=\operatorname{ord}_x(P')+1$, and hence
\begin{multline*}\operatorname{ord}_x\left(F\right)=\operatorname{ord}_x\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \beta_i u^{r_i-r_{k+1}}\right)\\=\operatorname{ord}_x\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k} (r_i-r_{k+1})\beta_i u^{r_i-r_{k+1}-1}\right)+1\leq k-1+1\end{multline*}
by the induction hypothesis. So the claim is established in dimension 1.

Now, let $F=\sum_{i=1}^T \beta_iu^{r_i}$ in the original context, assume without loss of generality that no $\beta_i$ vanishes, and suppose that $F(x)=0$ for $x=(x_1, ..., x_m)\in (\mathbb{C}^\times)^m$. For exponents $s_i\in \mathbb{Z}$ to be determined, set
\[\psi(t)=(x_1 t^{s_1}, ..., x_mt^{s_m}),\]
and note that
\[F\circ \psi (t)=\sum_{i=1}^T \beta_i x^{r_i} t^{r_i\cdot s},\]
where $r_i\cdot s$ is the usual dot product with $s=(s_1, ..., s_m)$, and
\[\operatorname{ord}_x(F)\leq \operatorname{ord}_{1}(F\circ\psi)\] by~\eqref{eq:orderpull}.
Thus we reduce to the 1-dimensional case as long as $F\circ \psi$ does not vanish identically, but the dot products $r_i\cdot s$ are distinct except on a finite union of hyperplanes in $\mathbb{Z}^m$, and so we can choose $s$ so that $F\circ\psi$ has the same number of non-zero terms as $F$.
head: environment

label: lem:super
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:super}
Let $R=\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r]$ and let $f(z)\in R[z]$ be monic, centred, and non-isotrivial. Then there is a super-attracting parameter $x\in \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r(\mathbb{C})$ for $f$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The claim follows in the stated generality from results of Dujardin and Favre~\cite{DF}, but in the interest of avoiding some technicalities, we apply these results in the case of dimension 1, and conclude the higher-dimensional statement by restricting to a curve.

In the case $r=1$, choose a smooth affine curve $B$ with a finite surjective map $B\to \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}$ such that every critical point $c$ of $f$ is defined over $\mathbb{C}[B]$. In a slight abuse of notation, we will also denote the pull-back of $f$ to $B$ by $f$. We are given that $f$ is non-isotrivial (which is true over $B$ given that it is true over $\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}$), so each $(f, c)$ is a holomorphic family of rational maps of degree $d$ with a marked critical point, as per~\cite{DF}. If every critical point $c$ were persistently preperiodic, then every fibre of the family would be PCF, and hence in the connectedness locus, which is compact in the space of monic centred polynomials~\cite{BH}. The coefficients of $f$ would then be bounded regular functions on $B$, hence constant, which is impossible given that $f$ is not isotrivial. So some critical point $c$ has infinite forward orbit on the generic fibre. By~\cite[Theorem~2.5]{DF}, the pair $(f, c)$ is not passive, since it is neither isotrivial nor persistently preperiodic, and then~\cite[Proposition~2.4 and its proof]{DF} gives a parameter $b_0\in B$ at which $c$ is periodic. The image of $b_0$ in $\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}$ is a super-attracting parameter.


Now consider the general case, with $a_i\in \mathbb{C}[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_r^{\pm 1}]$.   If $a_i(u)=\sum_{j=1}^{e_i} \gamma_j u^{r_{i, j}}$, note that the conditions $\beta\cdot r_{i,j}=\beta\cdot r_{i', j'}$ for $r_{i, j}\neq r_{i', j'}$ define finitely many hyperplanes in $\mathbb{Z}^r$, so we can choose  $\beta\in\mathbb{Z}^r$ with the dot products $\beta\cdot r_{i,j}$ distinct when the $r_{i, j}$ are, and with $\beta\cdot r_{i,j}\neq 0$ when $r_{i,j}\neq 0$. Let $\phi(t)=(t^{\beta_1}, ..., t^{\beta_r})$, which defines a map $\psi:\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m} \to \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r$. The polynomials $\phi^*a_i\in \mathbb{C}[t^{\pm 1}]$ have the same number of distinct monomials as the corresponding $a_i$, and non-constant monomials remain non-constant, and so in particular the $\phi^*a_i$ are not all constant. For monic centred polynomials, being isotrivial is the same as having constant coefficients, so the family $z^d+\phi^*a_{d-2}(t)z^{d-2}+\cdots +\phi^*a_0$ is not isotrivial. Now let $X\to \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r$ be a finite cover on which the critical points $c_1, ..., c_{d-1}$ of $f$ are regular functions, and let $B$ be the normalization of an irreducible component of $X\times_{\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r}\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}$ (fibre product over $\phi$) dominating $\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}$. Applying the previous case on $B$, some $c_i|_B$ has infinite forward orbit and is periodic at some $b_0\in B$. Then $c_i$ has infinite forward orbit on $X$, since a relation $f^n(c_i)=f^m(c_i)$ on $X$ would restrict to $B$, and the image of $b_0$ in $X$ lies above $x=\phi(t_0)$, where $t_0$ is the image of $b_0$ in $\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}$. So $x$ is a super-attracting parameter for the original family.
head: environment

label: lem:W
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:W}
Let $R=\mathbb{C}[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_m^{\pm 1}]$, and let $f(z)=z^d+a_{d-2}z^{d-2}+\cdots + a_0\in R[z]$ be a monic centred polynomial. If $S$ is the multiset of critical points of $f$ with infinite forward orbit (over the algebraic closure of the field of fractions of $R$), and 
\[W_{\ell, k}:=\prod_{c \in S}(f^{\ell}(c)-f^k(c)),\]
then $W_{\ell, k}\in R$, and $W_{\ell, k}\neq 0$ for $\ell\neq k$. If the $a_i$ lie in $k_0[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_m^{\pm 1}]$ for some subfield $k_0\subseteq \mathbb{C}$, then so does $W_{\ell, k}$. Furthermore, if $x$ is a super-attracting parameter, then there is a  $q$ such that
\[\operatorname{ord}_x(W_{q(\ell+1), q\ell})\geq \ell+1\]
for all $\ell\geq 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we confirm that that $W_{\ell,k}\in R$. Let $F$ be the field of fractions of $R$, and let $\overline{F}$ be its algebraic closure. Note that if $c \in \overline{F}$ is a critical point of $f$ with infinite forward orbit, then $\sigma(c)$ has this property for all $\sigma\in \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)$, and so we can factor $f'(z)=A(z)B(z)$ in $F[z]$ such that $B(c)=0$ if and only if the orbit of $c$ under $f$ is finite. As the roots of $f'(z)/d$ are integral over $R$, which is integrally closed, we have in fact $f'(z)=A(z)B(z)$ in $R[z]$, with $A$ monic, without loss of generality. It then follows that
\[W_{\ell, k}:=\prod_{c \in S}(f^{\ell}(c)-f^k(c))=\operatorname{Res}(A(z), f^\ell(z)-f^k(z))\in R,\]
just because the resultant is the determinant of a matrix with entries in $R$. The same argument, with $F$ replaced by the field of fractions of $k_0[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_m^{\pm 1}]$, shows that $W_{\ell, k}$ has coefficients in $k_0$ if the $a_i$ do. We have $W_{\ell, k}\neq 0$ for $\ell\neq k$ simply because none of the terms in the product vanish.


Now, let $x$ be a super-attracting parameter, so that there is a critical point $c$ with infinite forward orbit, hence a root of $A$, and a point above $x$ (on some finite cover) at which the reduction $\bar{c}$ of $c$ is periodic, of period dividing some $q\geq 1$. Write $g=f^q$ and
\[H(X, Y)=\frac{g(X)-g(Y)}{X-Y}\in R[X, Y],\]
so that
\[g^{n+1}(z)-g^n(z)=\left(g^n(z)-g^{n-1}(z)\right)H\left(g^n(z), g^{n-1}(z)\right).\]
Since the resultant is multiplicative, setting
\[Q_n=\operatorname{Res}\left(A(z), H\left(g^n(z), g^{n-1}(z)\right)\right)\in R\]
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prodf}W_{q(n+1), qn}=W_{qn, q(n-1)}Q_n\end{equation}
for all $n\geq 1$. Since $A$ is monic, these resultants are products of values of polynomials at the roots of $A$, and so they vanish at $x$ as soon as the two polynomials have a common root modulo the point above $x$. Now $A(z)$ and $g(z)-z$ have the common root $\bar{c}$ modulo this point, so $W_{q, 0}$ vanishes at $x$. Similarly, $\bar{g}^n(\bar{c})=\bar{g}^{n-1}(\bar{c})=\bar{c}$ and
\[\bar{H}(\bar{c}, \bar{c})=\bar{g}'(\bar{c})=0,\]
since $(f^q)'(z)$ has $f'(z)$ as a factor and $f'(\bar{c})=0$. So $Q_n$ vanishes at $x$ for all $n\geq 1$, and by~\eqref{eq:prodf} and induction
\[\operatorname{ord}_x(W_{q(\ell+1), q\ell})\geq \ell+1\]
for all $\ell\geq 0$.
head: environment

label: lem:trim
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:trim}
Let $K'/K$ be a finite extension, let $a_{d-2}, ..., a_0\in K'[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_r^{\pm 1}]$, and let $T\subseteq ((K')^\mathrm{cyc})^r$ be an infinite set of points at which the $a_i$ are regular, whose coordinates are all zero or roots of unity, such that $f_{t_0}$ is PCF for every $t_0\in T$, and such that $t_0\mapsto f_{t_0}$ is injective. Then there exists an exceptional family of dimension at most $r$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction on the number $n$ of coordinates such that there exists a point of $T$ with a zero in that coordinate. Of course, if $n=0$ then these data already define an exceptional family.

Now suppose that $n\geq 1$, and without loss of generality, suppose that the $r$th coordinate of some point in $T$ contains a zero. Let $T'\subseteq T$ be the subset consisting of those points whose $r$th coordinate is non-zero. If $T'$ is infinite, then we may replace $T$ by $T'$ and find ourselves in the previous case of the induction. Suppose $T'$ is finite. Since each $a_i$ is regular at some point of $T\setminus T'$, where $u_r=0$, no $a_i$ involves a negative power of $u_r$, and so we may set $b_i=a_i(u_1, ..., u_{r-1}, 0)\in K'[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_{r-1}^{\pm 1}]$ and take $S$ to be the projection of $T\setminus T'$ onto the first $r-1$ coordinates. This projection is injective, since the last coordinate vanishes on $T\setminus T'$, so $S$ is infinite, the $b_i$ are regular at the points of $S$, and the specializations of $z^d+b_{d-2}z^{d-2}+\cdots +b_0$ at points of $S$ are exactly the specializations of the original family at points of $T\setminus T'$. So we again find ourselves in the setting of the induction hypothesis.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K$ be a number field, and suppose that there are infinitely many monic centred PCF maps with coefficients in $K^{cyc}$. We will construct an exceptional family, in which the $a_i$ are in fact linear forms. 

Let $m$ and $e_1, ..., e_m\in K$ be the quantities ensured by Lemma~\ref{lem:DZ} applied to the adelic constant of Proposition~\ref{prop:house}, and consider the variety
\[Y\subseteq \mathbb{A}^{d-1}\times \mathbb{A}^{(d-1)m}\]
cut out by the equations
\[a_i = \sum_{j=1}^m e_j y_{i, j}.\]
For any tuple $(a_{d-2}, ..., a_0)\in K^{cyc}$ defining a PCF map, there is a point $y\in Y$ whose coordinates $y_{i, j}$ are all either $0$ or roots of unity, and we choose one such of each to obtain a set $T_0$ with the property that each tuple $(a_{d-2}, ..., a_0)$ is the projection of exactly one point in $T$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:trim} to the linear forms $\sum_j e_j y_{i, j}$ and the set of $y$-coordinates of points of $T_0$ give us an exceptional family.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M=M(d)$ be the adelic constant from Proposition~\ref{prop:house}.
Suppose that there is at least one exceptional family, and choose one of minimal dimension $r\geq 1$. Thus we have a finite extension $K'/K$, a tuple of Laurent polynomials $a_{d-2}, ..., a_0\in K'[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_r^{\pm 1}]$, and an infinite set $T\subseteq (\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r)^{\mathrm{Tors}}$ with the properties described above.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:DZ}, applied over $K'$ to the adelic constant $M_v^{d-1}$, there is for some $m'\geq 1$ a linear form
\[L(x_1, ..., x_{m'})=e_1x_1+\cdots + e_{m'}x_{m'}\in K'(x_1, ..., x_{m'})\]
such that every $\alpha\in (K')^\mathrm{cyc}$ with $|\alpha|_v\leq M_v^{d-1}$, for all $v$, can be written as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reps}\alpha = \sum_{i=1}^{m'} e_i \zeta_i,\end{equation}
with $\zeta_i\in \mu_\infty\cup\{0\}$. Since the $f_{t_0}$ are distinct for $t_0\in T$, and each conjugacy class contains only finitely many monic centred polynomials, the family is not isotrivial, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:super} there is a super-attracting parameter $y$ for $f$, and an associated period $q$. Let $W=W_{q(m'+1), qm'}$ in the notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:W}, and consider the, write $\pi: \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r\times \mathbb{A}^{m'}\to \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r$ for projection onto the first coordinate, and consider the equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Wpi}W(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{m'} e_i y_i,\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:W} with $k_0=K'$ we have $W\in K'[u_1^{\pm 1}, ..., u_r^{\pm 1}]$, so $W(t_0)\in (K')^\mathrm{cyc}$ for any $t_0\in T$. Since $W(t_0)$ is a product of at most $d-1$ differences $f_{t_0}^n(c)-f_{t_0}^m(c)$ with $c$ a critical point of $f_{t_0}$, Proposition~\ref{prop:house} gives $|W(t_0)|_v\leq M_v^{d-1}$ for all $v$, and so there is a point $s\in \pi^{-1}(t_0)$ such that the coordinates $y_i(s)$ consist of 0s and roots of unity. Let $S_0$ be a set constructed by choosing one such $s$ above each $t_0\in T$, noting that $f_{\pi_1(s)}$ are distinct as $s\in S_0$ varies.

Now, let $I_0= \{1, ..., m'\}$. For each $j\geq 1$, if there are infinitely many $s\in S_{j-1}$ with $y_j(s)\neq 0$, let $S_j\subseteq S_{j-1}$ be the set of all such points and let $I_j=I_{j-1}$. Otherwise, let $S_j$ be the set of points $s\in S_{j-1}$ with $y_j(s)=0$ and let $I_j=I_{j-1}\setminus \{j\}$. In the end, we have constructed a, infinite set $S_{m'}\subseteq S_0$ with the property that $y_j(s)\neq 0$ for all $s\in S_{m'}$ and $j\in I_{m'}$, and $y_j=0$ for all $s\in S_{m'}$ and $j\not\in I_{m'}$. For convenience, re-order the indices so that $I_{m'}=\{1, ..., m''\}$ and let $T'=\{(\pi(s), y_1(s), ..., y_{m''}(s)):s\in S_{m'}\}\subseteq \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r\times \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^{m''}$. We then have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ws}W(\pi(s))=\sum_{i=1}^{m''} e_i y_i(s)\end{equation}
for all $s\in S_{m'}$, the coordinates of all points in $T'$ are roots of unity, and the projection $\pi_1:T'\to T$ onto the first $r$ coordinates is injective. 


By Laurent's Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent} there is a positive-dimensional coset $\omega\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r\times \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^{m''}$ such that $T'\cap \omega\Gamma$ is dense in $\omega\Gamma$.
Suppose first that $P=\pi_1(\omega\Gamma)\neq \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r$. Then $P$ is a torsion coset of dimension $r'<r$. If $r'=0$ then $P$ is a point, and since $\pi_1$ is injective on $T'$, the set $T'\cap\omega\Gamma$ would contain at most one point, contradicting its density in the positive-dimensional $\omega\Gamma$. So $r'\geq 1$, and there is an isomorphism $\phi:\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^{r'}\to P$, defined over some extension $K''/K'$ obtained by adjoining finitely many roots of unity, specifically a map of the form
\[\phi(w)=(\omega_1 w^{v_1}, ..., \omega_{r}w^{v_{r}}),\]
where $v_i$ are exponent vectors and $\omega_i$ are roots of unity. We claim that the Laurent polynomials $b_i=\phi^* a_i$ and the set $T''=\phi^{-1}(\pi_1(\omega\Gamma\cap T'))$ form an exceptional family of dimension $r'<r$.

To see this, note that $b_i\in K''[y_1^{\pm 1}, ..., y_{r'}^{\pm 1}]$ by construction, and $T''$ is infinite since $\omega\Gamma$ contains infinitely many points of $T'$, and $\pi_1$ is injective on $T'$. The points of $T''$ are torsion, since $\phi$ is an isomorphism given by monomials times roots of unity. Also, the specialization of $z^d+b_{d-2}z^{d-2}+\cdots +b_0$ at $t_0\in T''$ is precisely the specialization of our original family $z^d+a_{d-2}z^{d-2}+\cdots + a_0$ at $\phi(t_0)\in\pi_1(T')\subseteq T$, so specializing at any $t_0\in T''$ yields a PCF polynomial, and the specialization map is injective because $\pi_1\circ \phi$ maps $T''$ injectively into $T$. So we have constructed an exceptional family of dimension $r'$, with $1\leq r'<r$, contradicting the minimality of $r$.

It must have been the case then that $\pi_1(\omega\Gamma)=\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^r$. Let $\phi:\mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^\sigma\to \omega\Gamma$ be an isomorphism, necessarily with $\sigma\geq r$, and write
\[\phi(w)=(\omega_1 x^{b_1}, ..., \omega_{\sigma}x^{b_{\sigma}}),\]
as above. Since~\eqref{eq:Ws} holds on a Zariski dense subset of $\omega\Gamma$, it holds on all of $\omega\Gamma$. Let $L=W\circ \pi\circ\phi\in K'[x_1^{\pm 1}, ..., x_\sigma^{\pm 1}]$. On the one hand, we have $L=\sum_{i=1}^{m''} e_i \omega_{r+i} x^{b_{r+i}}$. Since $\pi\circ\phi$ is surjective, it is dominant, so pulling back by it is injective and $L\neq 0$ because $W\neq 0$. In particular $m''\geq 1$, and $L$ is a non-zero Laurent polynomial with at most $m''\leq m'$ terms. It follows that $\operatorname{ord}_x(L)\leq m'-1$ for any $x\in \mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^\sigma$, by Haj\'os' Lemma~\ref{lem:hajos}.

On the other hand, $y\in \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^r$ is the super-attracting parameter chosen above, and $\operatorname{ord}_y(W)\geq m'+1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:W}. Since $\pi$ and $\phi$ are surjective over the algebraic closure, there is an $x\in \mathbb{G}_\mathrm{m}^\sigma$ with $\pi\circ\phi(x)=y$, and
\[m'-1\geq \operatorname{ord}_x (L)=\operatorname{ord}_x(W\circ\pi\circ\phi)\geq \operatorname{ord}_{\pi\circ\phi(x)}(W)=\operatorname{ord}_y(W)\geq m'+1.\]
This is a contradiction.
